title: The Gray Code

concept.title: Reflect the smaller list
body: A **Gray code** is an order of all binary strings of length `n` in which each string differs from the next one in exactly one position. There is a beautiful recursive way to build it: take the Gray code of length `n - 1`, put a `0` in front of every string; then take the same list **in reverse order** and put a `1` in front of every string; write the two lists one after the other.

Why does it work? Inside each half the neighbours differ in one place because the smaller list already does. Where the halves meet, the last string of the first half and the first string of the second half are the **same** string of length `n - 1` (that is why the list is reversed), and they differ only in the new first character. For `n = 2` the list is `00 01 11 10`.

statement: The Gray code of length 0 is the list with one empty string. The Gray code of length `n` is: every string of the Gray code of length `n - 1` with `0` added in front (in the same order), followed by every string of the Gray code of length `n - 1` with `1` added in front, in reverse order. Print the Gray code of length `n`, one string per line.

examples.note: The list is 000 001 011 010 110 111 101 100: neighbours differ in one place.

hints: The Gray code of length 0 is a list with one empty string.
Build the list for n from the list for n - 1: first the strings with 0 in front, then the reversed list with 1 in front.
Compute the smaller list once and use it twice.

explanation: The list for `n` is the list for `n - 1` with `0` in front, followed by the same list reversed with `1` in front. The two halves meet at the same string, so neighbours always differ in one place.
solution.complexity: Time O(2^n * n), space O(2^n * n).

code.python:
def gray(n):
    if n == 0:
        return [""]
    smaller = gray(n - 1)
    return ["0" + code for code in smaller] + ["1" + code for code in reversed(smaller)]

n = int(input())

print("\n".join(gray(n)))
